fatal_errors: The as-deposited material is incorrectly described as an ordered hexagonal phase with a first-order magnetostructural transition; the target films and nanoribbons were amorphous or extremely fine/disordered, with only cubic-type short-range order.
The proposed grain-boundary and phase-interface disorder mechanism presupposes grains, phase boundaries, and transformation nucleation that were not present in the as-deposited target state.

Annealing is predicted to introduce disorder and reduce the entropy-change peak, whereas 700 K annealing produced short-range atomic reordering and strain relaxation and increased magnetization and peak entropy change without detectable crystallization.
The proposed sharp transition and its hysteresis are not an appropriate baseline for the broad magnetic-cluster response of the deposited films and nanoribbons.
No prior observations or cited evidence support the claimed mediator or mechanism.
explanation: The response selects annealing below recrystallization as a controlled intervention and offers a nominally falsifiable annealing series, so it has limited intervention overlap and some experimental testability. However, it imports the ordered, first-order magnetostructural behavior of bulk material into an as-deposited amorphous thin-film system. The target mechanism is short-range reordering and relaxation of fabrication-induced strain, which lowers magnetic pinning barriers and improves collective ferromagnetic alignment; geometry and elastic magnetoelastic strain provide additional controls. The generated hypothesis instead invokes increased interface disorder and easier structural-transition nucleation, predicting broadening, reduced hysteresis, and a lower entropy-change peak. Those predictions conflict with the observed enhancement of magnetization and the increase of maximum −ΔSM from about 1.25 to 1.35 J kg−1 K−1 after 700 K annealing. It also omits the decisive ribbon-spacing and elastic-strain controls and uses measurement conditions that do not reconstruct the target protocol.
